14.0.s.en: 1. Chastity of the tongue and its sanctification

14.0.0.en: 1 Blessed is the man who has not slipped with his mouth, and is not stung by remorse for sin. 2 Blessed is he whom his conscience has not condemned, and who has not fallen from his hope.

14.0.1.en: Blessed is the man who does not slip and fall because of his mouth, and is not stung with pain because of his sin! [1]

14.0.2.en: Sirach begins his discourse on chastity and holiness with the chastity of the tongue and its sanctification. For if sin corrupts a person's inner peace, those who desire chastity and holiness are often preoccupied with ridding themselves of evil, lustful thoughts, especially the young, and they count deliverance from them exceedingly difficult. But Sirach holds the key to the thought that causes looseness of the tongue among friends. For under the cover of "love, friendship and familiarity," a person does not realize the importance of the sanctity of speech and conversation, even in times of merriment, entertainment or jesting. It befits the believer, as an ambassador of the Lord Christ, to place in his heart that he is always in the presence of God, and to ask that God's grace work in him, so that every good word comes forth for the edification of his own soul and the edification of his friends, and indeed of society. He is a man of God! The Apostle James speaks of the tongue as a small member, yet like the small rudder that steers the whole ship. Our life on earth is a period of training in the school of life, how to enjoy the sanctification of the tongue, so that by grace it may direct the whole being of man to enjoy the eternal heavenly wedding.

14.0.3.en: v Surely "Blessed is the man who does not slip with his mouth, and is not stung by remorse for sin" [1], or at least repents of the sins of the tongue [1].

14.1.0.en: v If we meet at feasts for the sake of love, and if the purpose of these festivals is to create a holy fellowship among the guests, and we use eating and drinking as instruments of love, does it not befit us to keep a manner that shows self-control of mind?... And if we gather in order to show good will toward one another, why do we stir up ill will through jesting and sport at the expense of others? Keeping silence is better than entering into a quarrel and using a coarse manner with error in deed. Surely: "Blessed is the man who does not slip with his mouth, and is not defiled by remorse for sin" (cf. Sir 14:1), or at least turns back from his sins that he committed by speech, or converses without causing pain to anyone [2].

14.1.1.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Many of the Fathers speak to us about the chastity of the senses and of all the members of the body:

14.1.2.en: v Striving to obtain perfect purity requires the striving of soul and body together in works of repentance, in harmony and equality. If the mind is granted some grace, it can then wrestle against the passions without relaxing or slackening, and receive the thoughts, directions and consolations of the Holy Spirit, and it can drive out of the soul the defiled inclinations that arise from the lusts of the heart. And by virtue of the fellowship between the mind or soul of man and the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit helps man to carry out the commandments he has learned, and guides him to drive all the passions out of the soul, whether those that arise from the soul itself independently of the body, or those that attached themselves to it by way of the body.

14.1.3.en: The Holy Spirit teaches man to keep his whole body - from head to foot - in harmony: he keeps the eyes so that they look with purity.

14.1.4.en: And he keeps the ears so that they listen in peace, or give heed to the things that belong to peace, without taking delight in talk about others, slanders and the disparagement of others.

14.1.5.en: And he keeps the tongue so that it speaks only what is good, giving weight to every word, and does not allow anything defiled or lustful to mix with its speech.

14.1.6.en: And he keeps the hands so that they move naturally, and are lifted up in prayer and in showing mercy and generosity.

14.1.7.en: And he keeps the stomach so that it has fitting limits for eating and drinking, according to the measure sufficient for the nourishment of the body, so that it does not let lust or gluttony turn it aside, and it exceed its limits.

14.1.8.en: And he keeps the feet so that they walk in righteousness according to the will of God, for the purpose of doing good works.

14.2.0.en: In this way the whole body becomes accustomed to every good work, and becomes subject to the authority of the Holy Spirit, and is gradually changed until it shares, to some extent, in the end in the qualities of the spiritual body that it receives at the just resurrection [3].

14.2.1.en: St. Anthony the Great v Adam was more glorious than a crown in his great beauty, and no other beauty was found among creatures to equal him.

14.2.2.en: His Maker set the two eyes of light on the top of the crown, that he might look at the creatures around him as from on high.

14.2.3.en: And He fashioned for him below two feet to run like a chariot, and by them he walks wherever he wishes to go.

14.2.4.en: And He fashioned at his sides two hands, with the ten fingers on them, by which he takes possession of sea and land and the whole world.

14.2.5.en: And He fashioned the brain, the house of the mind, to be there, and to dwell in the upper story like a god.

14.2.6.en: And He made for him a palate to examine foods, and set taste in it to distinguish between the sweet and the bitter.

14.2.7.en: And He opened the sense of smell to be a path for scents, by which he perceives (distinguishing) the foul odor from the pleasant.

14.2.8.en: And He pierced the hearing, and surrounded it with the pattern of the snail, that sounds might circle in it and enter with delight.

14.2.9.en: In his breast the heart, in which all thoughts are gathered, to distribute all the treasures as from a great treasury.

14.2.10.en: In his mouth the word, and in his lips the distinguishing of sounds, and the forehead as a sign; and He adorned the hollow of the eye with the two eyelids...

14.2.11.en: The Wise One of the worlds composed and arranged a different function in each member in the image of beauty when He perfected it.

14.3.0.en: The Creator made from nothing something great, that he might become lord of all things by wisdom [4].

14.3.1.en: v When the Creator created the mouth, He placed in it voice and word, that it might move to praise.

14.3.2.en: So everyone who feels the existence of the Creator must praise the Lord who created him.

14.3.3.en: The mouth of man is not given authority to use trivial news and unseemly words.

14.4.0.en: When the Creator created the mouth, He perfected it for His praise, and not to utter vain things [5].

14.4.1.en: St. Jacob of Serugh "and is not stung with pain because of his sin" [1].

14.4.2.en: We expected Ben Sirach, as he pronounced blessed the one who does not slip with his mouth, to say: "but keeps his tongue holy," but instead he said: "and is not stung because of his sin." Why? He warns us against the extreme of looseness in vain or evil speech, even if it is a sort of jesting, and against excess in grief and pain while offering repentance for every idle word. For just as frivolity is a danger to the holy life, so also remorse without hope destroys a person.

14.4.3.en: Ben Sirach often speaks of the joy of the Spirit even with the shedding of the tears of repentance, because hope drives a person to move constantly toward the pledge of heaven while we are still in this world.

14.4.4.en: Blessed is he whom his own soul does not condemn, and who has not been disappointed in his hope [2].

14.4.5.en: Control of the tongue with a spirit of joyful hope: it is good for a person to condemn himself for the looseness of his tongue, but while he offers repentance with tears of remorse, these tears are mingled with tears of joyful hope, because he meets the Forgiver of sins and Sanctifier of souls from corruption. The Apostle Paul warned us not to do anything with murmuring, lest we fall into the pit of despair. So it was with Judas, who repented and cast down the silver before those who had delivered him over, but did not open his heart in hope to the Savior of mankind as Simon Peter did, who said: "Lord, thou knowest that I love thee" (Jn 21:15).

14.4.6.en: This is what St. John the Beloved affirms when he says: "If our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart" (1 Jn 3:20). That is, if our inner life declares to us that our motives are not sound, let us cast ourselves upon God, confessing to Him our weakness in spite of the praise of men for us, and He is greater than our hearts, for He alone is able to set right our motives.

14.5.0.en: 3 Riches are not becoming to the miserly man, and what is the profit of wealth to an envious man? 4 He who gathers at the loss of his own soul gathers for others, and another will revel in his goods.

14.5.1.en: Wealth does not suit the narrow-minded man, and what is the purpose of money to the envious man? [3]

14.5.2.en: After warning us against looseness of the tongue, he warned us against looseness of thought and its lack of breadth. For in a life of frivolity a person does not care about the sanctity of his tongue, and through narrowness of mind he does not seek what is heavenly and eternal, but is occupied with gathering money, looking at heavenly things as imagination, an escape from reality and a loss of happiness. On the other hand, Ben Sirach links narrowness of mind with miserliness. For the miserly person's mind is narrow, so he does not practice giving with joy, and if he does practice it, it is under great pressure. Some reach such miserliness that they deprive themselves even of the necessities, and so they gather a fortune that others use, whether by seizing it, or by squandering it unwisely, or by leaving it to heirs after their death.

14.6.0.en: For he who gathers for himself gathers for others, and another enjoys his goods [4].

14.6.1.en: The miser desires to gather for himself all the possessions he can, and is seized with envy, desiring to acquire for himself what others have, and suffers from a constant thirst for all that is in the hands of others. So it is hard for him to give, but he always wants to take; therefore the Lord Christ said: "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (Acts 20:35).

14.7.0.en: v He who loves sin loves many possessions, and neglects righteousness, and does not think of the passing of life and its instability and the shortness of its term, and does not remember the certainty of death, which cannot be bribed. And if a person shows this shamelessness and lack of feeling until he reaches old age, he is like a rotten tree of no use [6].

14.8.0.en: 5 He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good? Does he not take no pleasure in his riches? 6 There is none worse than he who envies himself; that is the recompense of his wickedness. 7 And if he does good, it is by oversight, and in the end he shows his wickedness. 8 There is none more wicked than he who envies with his eye, and turns away his face, and despises souls. 9 The eye of the miser is not satisfied with his portion, and the iniquity of the wicked dries up his soul. 10 The evil eye envies bread, and at his own table he is in want.

14.8.1.en: Sirach highlighted the harm a person does to himself when he practices unholy conduct, such as:

14.8.2.en: a. Money possesses him instead of his possessing money [5].

14.8.3.en: b. He is miserly even to himself [6].

14.9.0.en: c. If he gives alms, it is without love [7].

14.9.1.en: d. He feels that what is in his brother's hand ought to have been his, so he envies his brother what he possesses.

14.9.2.en: He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?

14.9.3.en: And he does not enjoy his wealth [5].

14.9.4.en: When a person enslaves himself to money, money becomes a god to him. And instead of money serving him, he becomes its captive. He rejoices for a while when his balance increases, and does not know that money is a tyrannical master. For its sake a person sometimes falls into anxiety, and because of it he sometimes loses tenderness and mercy toward his brother. It brings him down from the joy of the Spirit to a state of disturbance. He loses the fruit of the Spirit, and deprives himself of moving freely toward heavenly things.

14.9.5.en: v If you look upon wealth and the perfect enjoyment of it as nothing but a deceptive show for a short time, and you know that the virtuous life that pleases God is better than wealth, and you hold fast to this belief and keep it in your memory, you will never groan or murmur or rebuke anyone, but will give thanks to God in every state, even if you see people worse than yourself praised for their eloquence or knowledge or wealth. The lust for wealth with greed, and pleasures, and the love of lust and vainglory, joined with ignorance of the truth, bring the worst sufferings of the soul [7].

14.9.6.en: St. Anba Anthony There is none worse than he who envies himself; that is the recompense of his vice [6].

14.9.7.en: In some translations the word "envies" came to mean being stingy, so one who is stingy toward himself is concerned with acquiring without spending for the salvation of his soul through giving; in this way he deprives himself of enjoying his wealth by hoarding it. Thus sin bears its fruit in itself, for he who envies himself, by enslaving himself to the love of possessions, receives the pledge of its fruit while still on earth, as he loses his inner peace and the joy of the Spirit.

14.9.8.en: And if he does good, it is without intention, and in the end he reveals his vice [7].

14.9.9.en: If he offers a kindness or alms from what he has by oversight, that is, not with the intention of giving joyfully, then when he corrects himself in the matter he shows his vice, that is, he reveals that he did not give the gift out of love. And since giving lacks the element of love, he loses his being and existence, and the person's life and growth are disrupted. The Apostle says: "And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor... and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing" (1 Cor 13:3).

14.9.10.en: v Give from what you own in righteousness, because you cannot offer a bribe to Christ your Judge.

14.10.0.en: v If you are sad as you give, you lose both the bread and the merit, because God loves a cheerful giver [8].

14.10.1.en: St. Augustine v If you stretch out your hand while your heart is empty of tenderness, you are doing nothing. The measure is not in the giving but in the joy in giving, and if there is no possibility of giving, tenderness alone is enough for those whom we love.

14.11.0.en: St. Anba Anthony v It is the intention that makes the gift precious or cheap [9].

14.11.1.en: St. Ambrose He is wicked who envies with his eye; he turns away his face and despises souls [8].

14.11.2.en: When a person envies his brother, counting that he is not worthy of what he has, he disdains his brother and despises him.

14.11.3.en: St. Basil the Great says that covetousness is the measure by which a person gauges his depths, whether covetousness has crept into them, and whether his love for himself is greater than his love for his neighbor.

14.11.4.en: v Question: By what measure is covetousness judged (Lk 12:15)?

14.12.0.en: Answer: When a person transgresses the limits set by the Law. According to the Old Testament this appears if a person thinks to take more than his neighbor, for it is written: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Lev 19:18; Mt 22:29). According to the Gospel, when one is concerned to take of the necessities more than he needs, beyond the need of the present day. Because of this someone heard: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God" (Lk 12:20-21) [10].

14.12.1.en: St. Basil the Great The eye of the greedy is not satisfied with his portion, and useless iniquity dries up the soul [9].

14.13.0.en: v It is said: "The eye of the greedy is not satisfied with his portion" (cf. Sir 14:9). Such a one cannot be corrected, and it is right to turn away from him [11].

14.13.1.en: St. John Chrysostom v Someone said: "No one is worse than lovers of money." This is the person who puts a price even on himself. He goes about like a public enemy of the world, complaining that the earth does not bear gold instead of wheat, or that there are springs instead of water channels, or mountains instead of stones. He is troubled if anyone gains a common benefit from anything.

14.14.0.en: He shuts every road that brings no monetary reward. He deals with anything from which he takes even two mites. He hates everyone, rich or poor. He hates the rich because he does not have what they have, and he counts all that others have as taken from him. It is truly his own, and he (the rich man) has seized it from him; so he is pleased with no one. He does not know the means of feeling abundance, and has no experience at all of being satisfied. He is the most wretched of all, as one who has nothing at all, and the practice of self-control is the thing most enviable to him [12].

14.15.0.en: v It is said: "The eye of the greedy is not satisfied with his portion" (cf. Sir 14:9)... For nature came into the world naked, and goes out of it naked. Therefore we do not seek luxuries, since we brought nothing with us, and we take nothing with us [13].

14.15.1.en: St. John Chrysostom The evil eye of a man envies his bread, and so he is in want at his table [10].

14.15.2.en: Envy is the natural fruit of selfishness, where a person wants to be the center of everything, and counts that he has the right to take from his brother what he has, even a crumb of bread. This selfishness strips him of the blessing of the Lord, so that instead of taking what is in his brother's hand, he loses even what he has. The envious person feels hunger and thirst, and there is no food or drink or possession that can satisfy him, even if he took the whole world in his hand.

14.16.0.en: 11 My son, spend on yourself according to what you have, and offer to the Lord offerings that are fitting for Him. 12 Remember that death does not delay. Has not the covenant of Hades been made known to you? 13 Before you die do good to your friend, and according to your ability stretch out your hand and give to him. 14 Do not lose a good day, and let not the portion of a good and desirable thing pass you by. 15 Shall you not leave your labors to another, and what you toiled for to be divided by lot? 16 Give and take, and justify your soul. 17 Before your death work righteousness, for there is no way to seek food in Hades. 18 All flesh wears out like a garment, for the covenant from the beginning is that it shall die the death. For as the leaves of a thick tree, 19 some fall and some grow, so is the generation of flesh and blood, some die and some are born. 20 Every corrupt work perishes, and its worker goes with it. 21 And every chosen work is justified, and its worker is honored for its sake.

14.17.0.en: My son, according to what you have treat yourself well, and offer to the Lord fitting offerings [11].

14.17.1.en: As Ben Sirach urges us toward the blessed life through the chastity of tongue, thought, conduct and so on, he urges our hearts toward the blessed heavenly life so that we may prepare for it. It is a celebration at an eternal level, where we meet the Bridegroom of souls, the Lord of glory Jesus, and it is a wedding that does not grow old or become ancient, but remains as though new throughout all eternity.

14.17.2.en: What occupies the human bride and groom in the last moments before the celebration of joy is the moments in which they unite to become one flesh; each forgets all his affairs for the sake of this lasting union. So our expectation of the heavenly wedding occupies us even above the needs of the body, as we see the heavenly Bridegroom preparing for us the eternal wedding. Even His heavenly servants await this great day with longing to see us a bride, a heavenly queen.

14.18.0.en: With every moment of eternity - if the expression is right - we feel as though for the first time we enjoy the mysteries of the glorious eternal wedding. On the Bridegroom's part, He offered His precious blood as a dowry for our souls, and on our part we offer Him offerings that are fitting for Him. What are these offerings but that we take of what is His and offer it to Him! During our life on earth, by striving that works through love. The Holy Spirit shapes us, and raises up from us the bride, the living icon of Christ. This is the daily offering according to His divine good pleasure. What are the offerings that are fitting for the Lord? 1. The offering of practical love: In a comment by St. John Chrysostom [14] on (Mt 5:23-24), "Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift," he says:

14.19.0.en: v What goodness this is! What surpassing love shown to mankind! For the sake of our love for our neighbor, He gave no importance to the honor due to Him. What saying is more tender than these words? He says: "Stop the service you offer Me, so that your love may continue. When you are reconciled with your brother, offer a sacrifice to Me." Yes, for this reason Jesus did not say "after the offering" but "before the offering." Rather, precisely, while the offering itself is there before you, He sends you to be reconciled with your brother... What is His motive for this immediate matter? It seems to me He has two aims that He indicates and prepares. First, He wishes to declare how much He exalts the value of love and counts it the greatest sacrifice, so that He does not accept the sacrifice of worship without the sacrifice of love. Second, He magnifies the necessity of reconciliation without leaving room for any excuse [15].

14.19.1.en: St. John Chrysostom 2. The offering of obedience: Another offering fitting for the Lord is obedience in the Lord. Saul thought that the Lord was pleased with burnt offerings, so Samuel said to him: "Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams" (1 Sam 15:22). 3. The offering of humility: "For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise" (Ps 51:16-18).

14.19.2.en: Remember that death does not delay, and that the covenant of the netherworld has not been revealed to you [12].

14.19.3.en: Death is a reality that no sensible person will ignore, and no one will know when it will come upon us, but it does not delay. Even if a person lives a thousand years, it is counted, in relation to eternity, as a drop of water from a sea or a grain of sand in a desert. To the bride it is a day of rejoicing in her wedding, and to the rebel he feels bitterness when he hears the name of death.

14.19.4.en: The principal clause of the covenant of the netherworld, or its charter, is that death comes upon a person without being bound to a set appointment, and it is not fulfilled according to man's desire.

14.19.5.en: Like all true sages, Ben Sirach reflects on the danger of being entangled in wealth, remembering the day of his death when he leaves all that he gathered or had to another. So it befits a person to spend on himself, that is, not to be preoccupied with hoarding it but to kindle it for his peace and his eternal salvation; therefore he offers to the Lord offerings fitting for Him as Creator and Savior and the One who cares for him.

14.19.6.en: v If the wicked man is converted and sighs, all his iniquities are no longer remembered (Ezek 18:21-22). It was also said: Do not postpone returning to the Lord. If the first promise gives you security, the second plea makes you anxious. Listen to the Holy Scripture, which says: "Remember, my son, that death does not delay" (cf. Sir 14:12), and do not say: "His mercy is great, and He will forgive the multitude of my sins. For with Him are mercy and wrath, and His indignation comes down upon sinners" (5:6-7), that is, those who persist in their sins. If we attend faithfully and carefully to the remedy of healing by repentance without delay, we can escape eternal punishment, and enjoy the eternal rewards.

14.19.7.en: Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v Dear beloved, let us think wisely and profitably about the judgment and the day of reckoning, with sighs and groans in sorrow over grave sins and faults throughout the days of our life...

14.19.8.en: v If you confess your sins, God forgives them to you. Let no one despair, and likewise let no one think of hope in a spirit of arrogance. The person who believes that even if he repents of his sins God's mercy will not forgive him sins by despair. As it was said to the despairing: "In the day in which the sinner returns, all his sins are forgiven" (cf. Ezek 18:21). As it is said to the arrogant: "Do not delay to turn to the Lord" (cf. Sir 5:7).

14.20.0.en: Beloved, may all people give heed to these words, men and women, clergy and laity, young and old, boys and girls [16].

14.21.0.en: v I urge you, as I often do, dear beloved, always to strive to think of the day of our death and the dreadful judgment. There is no remedy so useful for the wounds of all sins as that each one remember the hour in which he departs from this world. So the Scripture says: "My son, remember that death does not delay" (cf. Sir 14:12), "Remember the end of your life and cease from enmity" (cf. Sir 28:6). If one pays careful attention how severe his examination will be before the judgment of Christ, where He repays each one according to his work (Mt 16:27), his sins and faults cannot bring him pleasure [17].

14.22.0.en: Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v It is impossible for us to escape death by any means. And since the wise truly know this, they practice the virtues and think of the love of God, and face death without sighs or fear or tears, thinking that death is on the one hand inevitable, and on the other hand that it frees us from the diseases to which we are subject in this life [18].

14.22.1.en: St. Anthony the Great Before you die do good to a friend, and according to your ability stretch out your hand and give to him [13].

14.22.2.en: As we prepare for the heavenly wedding, it befits us to offer to the heavenly Bridegroom what is fitting for Him [11], and to realize that the wedding will not delay, for the hour of our departure from the world has drawn near [12]. We need to take delight in the Bridegroom until the last moments of our life on earth by giving to our brothers, especially the brothers of the Lord [13]. It is good for the believer to use his wealth in practical love for his friend, stretching out his hands in giving as far as he is able, before he dies and every opportunity for him passes away.

14.22.3.en: Do not allow a day to pass without a good deed, and do not let the carrying out of a good desire escape you [14].

14.22.4.en: Our life is a series of opportunities for preparing for the wedding; we must not allow time to play with us as though we were a ball in its hand; in the morning we say we shall do good at night, and at night we postpone it till tomorrow, and so time makes sport of us.

14.22.5.en: God placed in the hearts of men an inclination toward eternity, and they are drawn to it even if one denies it in his conversations with others. This inclination is what enables him to interpret temporal events, and reveals to him God's plan for him and for all humanity. Without the expectation of eternity, humanity loses its mission and its hope and lives in a state of confusion.

14.22.6.en: v Do not give all the days to iniquity; as long as you have authority, set aside time for righteousness.

14.23.0.en: We sinned yesterday; let us weep today over our crimes, lest sin spread and destroy us [19].

14.23.1.en: v Look at the day, how swift it is! And contemplate the night, how it pursues! Though they are quiet, they are busy with their works, and though they promise nothing, they carry out their tasks. They do not speak, and they complete their course. If the sun promised to rise and did not rise, it would not have lit the world by words (that is, by a bare promise)...

14.24.0.en: v Works are not accomplished by words (promises). Creatures come into being by deeds. The sun rises while silent, and lights the earth without speaking. So say nothing without doing it, but do what you say [20].

14.25.0.en: v If a good thought comes to you in the evening, begin to carry it out that night. And if the memory of good things awakens in you in the morning, do not refrain from doing good deeds, because the day does not prevent you from completing your works. Attend to your work before the day goes down [21].

14.25.1.en: v Do not close your eyes in slumber without having opened your mind to prayer. You have seen how the day was hurrying to go; hasten to leave your sins with it! And let your righteousness rise with the morning! Do not put off today's work until tomorrow.

14.26.0.en: v Behold, the days are buried like the dead. Yesterday we buried yesterday, and here we advise today that it will also be of benefit. Weep, then, over yesterday, which no longer exists, and raise your voice over today, for it too will pass away. Behold, the days snatch you away, and life flees. When the evening buries you, the morning raises you. They put you to death daily so that you may know that you will die [22].

14.26.1.en: v Yesterday's life has fled from you, and here today's life is quickly passing. Whether you are awake or asleep, the night does not stop its course, and the day does not rest from completing the journey of its way.

14.27.0.en: Your life here is being plundered, so plunder from it the benefit. Do not rely on the morning because it is bright, if your mind is not enlightened by God so that it may shine. Do not think the evening is for rest, as long as your soul is tormented by the pains of evils [23].

14.27.1.en: v Until today you have not been your own king, but a slave of the world. Be king over yourself, and serve it...

14.28.0.en: If a thief robbed you, you would wail, while your life is being stolen from the life of God and you do not grieve over it [24].

14.28.1.en: St. Jacob of Serugh Will you not leave all the toil of your work to another, and the fruit and all the toil of your work to be divided by lot? [15]

14.28.2.en: A time comes for every person when work ceases, as he departs from this world, and all that he owned becomes an inheritance for others.

14.28.3.en: Give and take and control yourself, for there is no way to seek luxury in Hades [16].

14.28.4.en: Giving is the sure way to receiving. The more we open our hearts and our storehouses to our brothers, the more we find the hand of God stretched out to give generously, and His storehouses open for us to draw from them.

14.28.5.en: All flesh wears out like a garment, for the covenant from the beginning is that "thou shalt surely die" [17].

14.28.6.en: v Of this wrath he says: "We were by nature the children of wrath, even as others" (Eph 2:3). And of it Jeremiah says: "Cursed be the day wherein I was born" (Jer 20:14). Of this wrath Job also says: "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble. He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down... and never continueth in the same state. And upon such an one thou hast opened thine eyes, and broughtest me into judgment with thee. Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one; though his life be but one day upon the earth" (Job 14:1-5) LXX... And of this wrath it is said in Ben Sirach: "All flesh wears out like a garment, for the law of the world from the beginning is that thou shalt surely die" (cf. Sir 14:17)...

14.29.0.en: Of this wrath came the voice of the Apostle: "The creature was made subject to vanity" (Rom 8:20). And of it the psalm laments: "Behold, thou hast made my days as an handbreadth, and mine age is as nothing before thee: surely every man is made a breath" (Ps 39:5) [25].

14.29.1.en: St. Augustine Like blossoming leaves on a thick tree, some fall and others grow, so also are the generations of flesh and blood: one dies and another is born [18].

14.29.2.en: v The human race is preserved by two bodily processes, to which the wise man and the saint submit as duties, while the fool rushes into them recklessly, led by his lust. And this one differs from the other. What are these two processes by which humanity is preserved? The first concerns us and relates to our nourishment, and this, without doubt, we cannot use except with some bodily pleasure. This is eating and drinking. If you do not eat and drink you die, because the human race lives by this aid according to the law of its nature. But this process is a provision that concerns individual persons only, for they do not obtain a successor by eating and drinking but by their marriage. So humanity is preserved first by the means of life, but however great their care, they cannot live forever; therefore another aid was given them by which the newborn take the place of those who die. For as it is written, the human race is like the leaves of the tree, or the olive, or the laurel, or other kinds of trees that are always in leaf, and yet the same leaf does not remain always [18]. For as it is written: "This one sheds and that one grows," because the new leaves that grow replace the others that fall. So the tree always sheds its leaves and yet is always covered with leaves. Thus humanity does not feel its loss of those who die day by day because of its being supplied with the newborn. Therefore all humanity is sustained according to its laws. And as leaves are always seen on trees, so the earth is seen full of people. Whereas if they were dying without others being born, the earth would be stripped of all its inhabitants as some kinds of trees are stripped of all their leaves [26].

14.29.3.en: St. Augustine Every work of man is corrupted and fails, and the man who does it departs with it [19].

14.30.0.en: 22 Blessed is the man who meditates on wisdom, and speaks of it in his mind, 23 and reflects on its ways in his heart, and considers its secrets. He goes after it like one who searches, and lies in wait at its entrances, 24 and looks through its windows, and listens at its doors, 25 and lodges near its house, and drives a peg into its wall, and pitches his tent beside it, and dwells in a lodging of good things. 26 He places his children under its shelter, and dwells under its branches. 27 He is sheltered by its shade from the heat, and in its glory finds rest.

14.30.1.en: Our life on earth is an opportunity for the constant seeking to obtain wisdom and to grow in it, as the bride who is preparing for union with the Bridegroom, the Wisdom of God! [20-27] It requires constant striving with care and diligence, like a hunter tracking the traces of a bird he wishes to catch. This striving touches the inner life of the believer and the sanctification of his thought. Through this earnest striving the believer finds delight in his life, because he is in the company of the Giver of wisdom, who protects him from the burning heat and grants him to enjoy the glory of wisdom [27].

14.30.2.en: Just as the bride thinks constantly of her bridegroom, to whom she returns love for love, and thinks of her married life with prudence, so the believer meditates on heavenly wisdom, and meditates on its way that leads him to the divine embrace, and seeks to know its secrets.

14.30.3.en: He does not stop at meditation but is always moving toward his heavenly Bridegroom, enjoying the company of the Lord, "the Wisdom of God," bearing Him within himself and imitating Him, and experiencing the pledge of his heavens like one who looks upon eternity while still in the flesh, going forth as from door to door, as Esther did when the doors were opened to her until she entered to the king's throne. The believer insists on living on earth as one who dwells in the house of the Lord, and pitches the cords of his tent as under the shadow of His care, and takes shelter in Him from the heat of trials, and tastes the inner glory by the indwelling of the Lord in him. He does not cease to pray that all may taste the sweetness of fellowship with the Savior.

14.31.0.en: The sage personifies wisdom as a maiden whom the believer seeks as a bride for himself: 1. He meditates on her to know her depths and glory, thinking prudently [20] how he may be united with her. 2. He reflects on her ways in his mind [21], to walk in Christ the royal road to the bosom of the Father. 3. He considers her secrets [21], that is, he enjoys the mind of Christ and comes to know His secrets. 4. He looks through her windows and listens at her doors [21]. He never tires of seeing the Lord and listening to His voice. 5. He pursues her like a hunter, and lies in wait for her traces. He will not cease to seek the Lord and to acquire Him, and to walk in Him. 6. He builds his house adjoining her house and drives the peg of his tent into her walls. He remains watchful to meet her. 7. He pictures her as a tree in which he takes shelter so that the sun of burning trials does not strike him. 8. He speaks of wisdom as a maiden he wishes to marry, and as a bird he wants to catch and fly away with, and as a beautiful queen with a sweet voice at whom he looks through the windows, and to whose voice he listens at the doors. And as a tree that protects him and shelters him from the heat, and another full of glory in which he wants to dwell, pouring her beauty and splendor upon him.

14.32.0.en: v It is written: "Wisdom is better than precious stones, and all precious things are not to be compared with it" (Prov 8:11) LXX. For the wisdom that comes down from above from God is a gift without parallel. And when we perceive it by means of the Holy Scripture inspired by God, and receive the divine light to dwell in our minds, we then advance without deviation to all that is profitable for our spiritual benefit [27].

14.32.1.en: St. Cyril the Great Blessed is the man who practices wisdom, and speaks with understanding [20].

14.32.2.en: And reflects on the ways of wisdom in his heart, and considers its secrets [21].

14.32.3.en: v The mind that lives in a soul that loves God sees in truth God, who is invisible and indescribable... sees God who alone is pure to the pure [28].

14.32.4.en: St. Anthony the Great He pursues her (wisdom) like a hunter, and lies in wait for her traces [22].

14.32.5.en: Origen sees that the last thing mentioned in the Book of Numbers is the command issued by God to Moses defining the boundaries of the land of Canaan on the four sides. And the simple reader understands this divine command to be of the utmost importance, to be kept literally so that no one transgresses these boundaries and seizes what is not his right. Now the Jews transgressed the boundaries when they were taken captive into exile outside Canaan or resorted to leaving Canaan and dwelt in other lands. What use, then, is this text to us, who are not Jews?

14.32.6.en: Origen answers that this text is symbolic and we must keep to it spiritually. It concerns wisdom, so it befits the believer to strive not to go outside the boundaries of heavenly wisdom. He seeks it that he may follow it with exactness and care, and it grants him understanding of the Holy Scriptures. This is what Paul the Apostle strove for, when he said that those who served the Law are servants of the shadow and image of heavenly things (Heb 8:5). All that is in the Law concerning material temporal things is a shadow of good things to come (Heb 10:8). The things the Law pointed to are good on earth, and are a shadow and image of the heavenly things [29].

14.32.7.en: And he looks through her windows with determination, and listens at her doors [23].

14.32.8.en: And he lodges near her house, and drives a peg into her walls [24].

14.32.9.en: In the preceding expressions [21-23] he speaks of seeking wisdom as one on a journey with its toils, and now in the following expressions [24-27] the journey turns into a dwelling with wisdom: the believer lodges near her house, that is, heaven, and drives a peg into her walls, that is, he is bound to the Church, which carries the pledge of heaven, and experiences with every morning his dwelling in wisdom, or his abiding in Christ the Wisdom of God and Christ's abiding in his depths, where He establishes His kingdom in him.

14.32.10.en: And he establishes his house according to her will, and dwells in a good lodging [25].

14.32.11.en: v This is the duty of those who are zealous for the good pleasure of God, to ask what is best for them to do [30].

14.32.12.en: St. Basil the Great He places his children under her protection, and takes refuge under her branches [26].

14.32.13.en: He takes shelter in her from the burning heat, and dwells in her glory [27].

14.32.14.en: In conclusion, the heavenly Bridegroom calls us to receive from Him the heavenly wisdom, which protects us from the heat of the trials of the world, and satisfies us with the pledge of the heavenly table, and pours its splendor upon us, so that we are enlightened while still in the world, and become a cause of wonder to the heavenly beings.

14.33.0.en: v Glory to You, who establish Your kingdom within us!

14.33.1.en: Who can turn my earthen heart into a heaven but You?

14.33.2.en: Set, O Lord, a strict guard over my mouth, that Your holy fragrance may appear in it, and every word be seasoned with Your Holy Spirit.

14.33.3.en: If my tongue slips with an unseemly word, grant me sincere repentance by the work of Your fiery Spirit.

14.33.4.en: So that I cry out with the Apostle: "Lord, You know that I love You!"

14.33.5.en: v Do not forsake me, lest I fall into hopelessness, so that instead of the joy of the Spirit I shatter myself with despair.

14.33.6.en: I confess to You: "I have sinned against You, O Forgiver of sins." Behold, sin wishes to shatter me.

14.33.7.en: Sanctify my thoughts, O Lord, that I may sing with the Apostle, saying: "We have the mind of Christ."

14.33.8.en: What a mind You grant me, You who desire the salvation of the world.

14.33.9.en: Grant me to enjoy breadth of mind, that I may seek the salvation of everyone.

14.33.10.en: Instead of envy killing me over the rich, let my soul groan over everyone whose heart is attached to temporal things.

14.33.11.en: I count all things loss that I may win You! And let my depths rejoice with the repentance of every person!

14.33.12.en: Let my mind not be narrowed by a spirit of blind fanaticism, and let my heart and mind not be bound to vain temporal things!

14.33.13.en: Is it hard for You to turn the earth into a rejoicing heaven?

14.33.14.en: Your divine presence in my depths carries me away to the heavens that are within me!

14.33.15.en: Come, O Savior, and declare Your constant presence in humanity.

14.33.16.en: v I thank You, who gave me even money as a gift from You, not that I may be attached to it, but that I may be attached to You.

14.33.17.en: You are my wealth and my riches, You satisfy all my needs.

14.33.18.en: Grant me to kindle all my talents, even money, for the account of Your heavenly kingdom.

14.33.19.en: Grant me that money may not possess me and enslave me, but that I may possess it and rule over it; open my heart to give generously and joyfully to my brothers, and by it I offer You sacrifices of thanksgiving, O my Creator.

14.33.20.en: v Grant me, O Lord, that my eyes may not look at what is in my brother's hand.

14.33.21.en: And that I may not desire to acquire what is his, but count what is in his hands as though it were with me, and rejoice for him!

14.33.22.en: Remove from me the spirit of covetousness and greed, for I was born naked and shall go out of the world empty-handed.

14.33.23.en: I did not enter the world with anything, and I hope to depart carrying You alone in my heart.

14.33.24.en: v My God, I see You coming on the clouds, to raise up the heavenly bride from Your believers.

14.33.25.en: You offered Your precious blood as a dowry for her; what, then, can we offer You but what You gave her by Your Holy Spirit!
